concepts.name: cancel() vs cancelAndJoin() and the cancelling state
Retrofit suspend functions: HTTP errors and cancellation
Migrating SharedPreferences to DataStore with DataMigration

choices.text: Nothing: `cancel()` suspends until the old job's `finally` has finished
`cancel()` returns at once; `cancelAndJoin()` waits for the job to end
`cancel()` also cancels the caller, so `startUpload()` is never reached
`cancel()` skips `finally` blocks, so `releaseFile()` never runs at all

questions.explanation: `cancel()` is not a suspending function: it moves the job to the cancelling state and returns immediately, while the job may still be running its `finally` block. `cancelAndJoin()` (cancel, then `join`) suspends until the job is complete. Cancelling a job is a normal cancellation and doesn't cancel the caller, and `finally` blocks do run.

sources.title: Job
sources.claim: `cancel` moves a job to the cancelling state immediately (isActive false, isCompleted false, isCancelled true), and it becomes cancelled only when it finishes its work and its children complete; `cancel` is a normal cancellation that doesn't cancel the parent.

sources.title: cancelAndJoin
sources.claim: `cancelAndJoin` cancels the job and suspends the invoking coroutine until the cancelled job is complete; it is a shortcut for `cancel` followed by `join`.

questions.prompt: A Retrofit service declares `@GET("users/{id}") suspend fun user(@Path("id") id: Long): User`, and the server answers `404`. What does the call do?

choices.text: It returns `null`, because the response has no body to convert into a `User`
It returns a `User` whose fields hold the default values from the class
It throws `HttpException`; a `Response<User>` return type would not
It throws `IOException`, the same as when the server can't be reached

questions.explanation: For a suspend function returning the body type, Retrofit resumes with the body only for a successful response and throws `HttpException(response)` otherwise. Declaring `Response<User>` returns the response whatever its status, so you can read `code()` and `errorBody()`. `IOException` is for failures to talk to the server, not HTTP error statuses.

sources.title: retrofit2/KotlinExtensions.kt (Retrofit source)
sources.claim: `Call.await()` resumes with the body for a successful response, resumes with `HttpException(response)` for an unsuccessful one, and registers `invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }` so cancelling the coroutine cancels the Call; `awaitResponse()` resumes with the Response whatever its status.

sources.title: Retrofit change log
sources.claim: Retrofit 2.6.0 added `suspend` service functions, which behave like `Call<User>` invoked with `enqueue`; you can also return `Response<User>` for access to the response metadata.

questions.prompt: A released app keeps its settings in SharedPreferences and is moving them to Preferences DataStore. How do you migrate existing users' values safely?

model_answer.summary: Give the DataStore a `SharedPreferencesMigration` through `produceMigrations`, which runs before any data is returned; keep migrations idempotent, never read the DataStore from inside one, and keep a single DataStore instance per file.
key_points: Pass a `SharedPreferencesMigration` (with the keys to migrate, all by default) through `produceMigrations`; DataStore returns no data until all migrations have completed
Migration methods can run more than once, so they must be idempotent; if `migrate` fails nothing is committed, `cleanUp` isn't called and the migration is retried on the next access
Don't read the DataStore inside `shouldMigrate` or `migrate`: it deadlocks, since DataStore waits for migrations to finish
Create one DataStore instance per file in the process (for example a top-level `preferencesDataStore` delegate); two instances for one file make reads and writes throw `IllegalStateException`

questions.explanation: DataStore's migrations are designed for exactly this move: they run on first access, before any reader sees data, and they are retried until they succeed. The risks are your own code: a non-idempotent migration that runs twice, a migration that reads the store it is migrating, or two instances fighting over one file.

sources.title: SharedPreferencesMigration
sources.claim: SharedPreferencesMigration is a DataMigration from SharedPreferences to DataStore that takes the SharedPreferences and a set of keys to migrate (all keys by default), and is passed to the DataStore builder through produceMigrations.

sources.title: DataMigration
sources.claim: shouldMigrate, migrate and cleanUp may be called multiple times so must be idempotent; if migrate fails nothing is committed, cleanUp isn't called and migration is retried on the next DataStore call; reading DataStore inside these functions deadlocks because DataStore doesn't return data until all migrations complete.

sources.title: DataStore
sources.claim: Never create more than one DataStore instance for a given file in the same process, or DataStore throws IllegalStateException when reading or updating; updateData is transactional; consider migrating from SharedPreferences to DataStore.

questions.prompt: Right after `job.cancel()`, while the coroutine is still running its `finally` block, what do `isActive`, `isCompleted` and `isCancelled` return?

choices.text: `false`, `false`, `true`: the job is in the cancelling state
`false`, `true`, `true`: the job is cancelled once `cancel()` returns
`true`, `false`, `false`: the job stays active until `finally` ends
`false`, `true`, `false`: it counts as completed but not cancelled

questions.explanation: `cancel()` moves the job to the transient cancelling state at once: not active, not yet completed, but `isCancelled` is true. It becomes cancelled, with `isCompleted` true, only when its work (including `finally`) and its children have finished, which is what `join()` waits for.

sources.title: Job
sources.claim: `cancel` moves a job to the cancelling state immediately (isActive false, isCompleted false, isCancelled true), and it becomes cancelled only when it finishes its work and its children complete; `cancel` is a normal cancellation that doesn't cancel the parent.

questions.prompt: `viewModelScope` is cancelled while a Retrofit `suspend fun feed(): Feed` call is in flight. What happens to the HTTP request?

choices.text: It keeps running, and its result is dropped when it eventually returns
It finishes first, because a suspend call can't be cancelled mid-request
Retrofit cancels the underlying OkHttp `Call` as the coroutine cancels
Retrofit retries it on the next `viewModelScope` that becomes active

questions.explanation: Retrofit's suspend support wraps the `Call` in `suspendCancellableCoroutine` and registers `invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }`. When the coroutine is cancelled, the OkHttp call is cancelled too, so leaving the screen stops the network work instead of letting it run to completion.

sources.title: retrofit2/KotlinExtensions.kt (Retrofit source)
sources.claim: `Call.await()` resumes with the body for a successful response, resumes with `HttpException(response)` for an unsuccessful one, and registers `invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }` so cancelling the coroutine cancels the Call; `awaitResponse()` resumes with the Response whatever its status.

questions.prompt: In a custom `DataMigration`, `migrate()` calls `dataStore.data.first()` to read the current settings. What happens?

choices.text: It deadlocks: DataStore returns no data until migrations finish
It reads the values stored before this migration was started
It throws `IllegalStateException`, since it made a second DataStore
It reads empty preferences, because migrations run on a blank file

questions.explanation: DataStore doesn't return data until all its migrations have completed, so reading it from inside `migrate` (or `shouldMigrate`) waits forever. Use the `currentData` parameter that `migrate` receives instead. Reading the same instance doesn't create a second DataStore.

sources.title: DataMigration
